newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP demands radical overhaul of transit system.
newsitem.headline: EP demands radical overhaul of transit system.

text.p: The European Parliament called on Thursday for a complete overhaul of the European Union's transit system to stem fraud estimated at several billion Ecus a year.
The call is included in a critical report from the parliament's special committee of inquiry into the Transit system, adopted by the parliament on Thursday.

The system allows goods lorries to cross EU countries and several neighbouring states tax free, only paying customs duties, value-added tax and excise duties at their final third- country destination.
But some operators forge documents and offload cigarettes, alcohol and other high value goods on the EU market. The goods never arrive in the city where the taxes must be paid.
The parliament's inquiry, which started in December 1995, was the first under new investigative powers granted to Euro-MPs by the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

It revealed the gaping contradiction between the EU's decision in 1993 to abolish internal borders so goods could circulate freely through the Union, and its failure to update its archaic paper-based customs system to come to grips with the change.

"Public authorities continue to see their role as stopping at national borders whilst economic operators, whether legal or illegal, have taken advantage of the new freedoms to full effect," the report says.
"Goods cross borders, criminals cross borders, profits from illegal activities cross borders, public authority stops at the borders."
The result has been vast profits for criminals from the EU's budget, national coffers and the pockets of the private companies who provide the guarantees for transit operations.
Edward Kellet-Bowman, the report's author, has said the total fraud could be worth up to 30 billion Ecus.
Parliament demanded a string of reforms to the system, which was designed in the 1960s for a European Community of only six members.

It now handles 18 million operations a year in the 15 EU states, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Iceland, Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, its neighbours in the European Free Trade Association and the Visegrad grouping.
First and foremost, the outdated and fragmented customs system had to be replaced immediately by a computerised network, for which the EU has already promised 50 percent of the money.

It was ridiculous to have services using rubber stamps which could be stolen or falsified, when it would cost a fraction of the money lost in fraud to instal a computer network, committee chairman John Tomlinson told a news conference on Wednesday.

Parliament said access to the transit system should be limited, particularly in relation to sensitive goods like alcohol and cigarettes, especially given the apparently ambiguous role of tobacco multinationals.

"We sought testimony from the tobacco multinationals. Some were willing to talk, but Philip Morris wanted part of their testimony kept confidential. I cannot say we were convinced by all the companies told us," Tomlinson said.
Euro-MPs urged the Joint Committee on Common Transit, which involves 23 European countries, to conduct a thorough investigation into cigarette trade and recommend sanctions against fraudsters.
Parliament's inquiry discovered that cigarette smuggling accounted for 19 percent of fraud and a massive 47 percent of lost tax revenue.
Euro-MPs said the customs code should be changed to permit spot checks on goods lorries anywhere on EU territory and a coordinated system of physical checks at land borders and ports.

They also demanded better cooperation between national prosecutors and said the European Commission's anti-fraud unit (UCLAF) should have the same powers as national authorities to initiate criminal proceedings.
In the long term, the ideal solution would be an EU-wide customs system backed up by a common investigative service based on UCLAF, Euro-MPs said.
It was also vital, they said, to get better cooperation from neighbouring countries like Switzerland, whose laws, notably those on banking secrecy, contributed to the problems of the transit system.

It was not for nothing that a quarter of all transit lorries passed through Switzerland, even cargoes of American cigarettes arriving in Antwerp and destined for Azerbaijan, Tomlinson told a recent news conference.
Parliament said the EU should use negotiations on trade and EU membership to press Switzerland, Cyprus and the countries of eastern and central Europe to tighten their transit rules.
The EU's decision last year to extend the transit system to the Visegrad countries had been extremely ill-advised, given the weaknesses of the system, the parliament report said.
